question: Where does the spectacle come from: apparatus the creator builds himself (menus, rigs, staged tests) or chaos harvested from other people and public spaces he does not control
pole_high: harvested from lobbies, strangers and public chaos
why: Neotastic's two videos split exactly here - a solo sandbox video is fully engineered while his public-lobby video is harvested - which the single engineered-to-emergent axis (spectacle-001) cannot express. Source and construction are different variables, and an avatar needs to know which game it is in
evidence_needed: Per-format shadings (lobby vs solo) for at least three spectacle creators, starting with Neotastic and Jesse Gillett

question: After the big destruction, how long does the creator stay with the wreck: touring it, inspecting it, reconstructing what happened, or cutting to the next setup within seconds
pole_low: gone in seconds, next setup already loading
pole_high: lingers as an investigator, the wreck gets its own segment
why: Neotastic tours his flooding ship with a flashlight and admires it underwater; GrayStillPlays gives every wreck one line and is gone. The aftercare beat decides whether destruction feels like evidence or confetti, and it shapes the avatar's whole failure rhythm
evidence_needed: Timed wreck-dwell measurements from at least three creators across the spectacle cluster (Neotastic, Jesse Gillett, GrayStillPlays)

question: When the creator's own character dies or is humiliated, how is the death treated: mourned in character as a real loss, or shrugged off as a throwaway gag with no weight at all
pole_low: death is a shrug, weightless by design
pole_high: death is mourned in character, grief is the bit
why: Neotastic grieves play-money losses at length in one video and treats his own death as an errand in the other; Gray treats every death as nothing. This is the personal end of stakes-001 and it is not the same dial as narrating costs for others
evidence_needed: Own-death segments from at least three creators, coded separately from other-stakes narration

question: How much of the commentary IS the count: money, multipliers, seconds, prices and tallies spoken as the main line, versus numbers mentioned only at milestones
pole_high: the count is the commentary, most lines carry a number
why: GrayStillPlays' clicker video is narrated by the tally, and Neotastic's comparison video runs on its price spine, while most creators treat numbers as punctuation. For an avatar in number-heavy games this decides whether the audience can follow the run at all
evidence_needed: Line-level counts of number-bearing commentary in one number-heavy and one number-light video per creator, at least three creators

question: Where does the warmth live: spread evenly through the ordinary minutes, or withheld during the run and concentrated into the closing minute
pole_low: even warmth, the whole video feels the same temperature
pole_high: cool or ironic run, warmth saved for the door
why: GrayStillPlays is wry for an hour and genuinely warm for the last minute of both sampled videos, and Neotastic's farewells do similar work. Warmth PLACEMENT is a structure a kid coach can actually choose, unlike warmth as a vague trait
evidence_needed: Warmth-coded segments per video third for at least three creators, closings included

question: How does chaos start: the creator provokes the game's own systems into misbehaving (testing rules, clipping, abusing physics) or authors scenarios with external tools, menus and spawns
pole_low: authors scenarios with tools and menus
pole_high: provokes the game's own systems until they break
why: Gray's first act is breaking the death rule to test it and his chaos is provoked from inside the game's rules; Neotastic's sandbox video is authored from menus while his lobby video is provoked by presence. Provocation reads as cleverness, authoring as power - the audience learns different things from each
evidence_needed: Chaos-initiation coding for the first three major incidents in videos from at least three creators

question: In multiplayer, how much of the runtime is managing other people - recruiting, reassuring, assigning, promoting, blaming - versus playing the game while others happen to be present
pole_low: others are background, the game is the content
why: Neotastic spends much of both videos running a crew: recruiting passengers, talking a griefer down, promoting a stand-in captain. The coach product is itself about directing others, so how a performer makes people-management entertaining is core curriculum, and no current question measures the share of runtime it takes
evidence_needed: Runtime-share estimates of people-management talk in multiplayer videos from at least three creators (Neotastic, OMB Gaming, Jesse Gillett)

question: Is prediction a sport: the creator calls outcomes before they land and keeps score of his own calls, versus pure reaction with no forecasting
pole_low: pure reactor, nothing is called in advance
pole_high: compulsive forecaster who scores his own predictions
why: Gray calls jump scares, falling beams and mechanics before they happen and collects the credit aloud; Neotastic forecasts sink outcomes and grades himself. Forecasting gives the audience a second game to play alongside the run, and it is a learnable avatar behaviour
evidence_needed: Prediction calls per video, hit or miss noted, for at least three creators
